title: Informal Conjecture (second phase transition for all radii)
statement_text: It seems likely that for every radius $r$ there should be a second phase transition around some threshold $t=t(n)$. By which we mean that, if $p=\omega(t(n))$, then $G\in\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is with high probability reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods, while if $p=o(t(n))$ and $p=\omega(n^{-\frac{2r+1}{2r}})$, then with high probability $G$ is not reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods.
context_text: For a graph $G$, a vertex $v$ and an integer $r\ge1$, the $r$-neighbourhood $N^{(G)}_r(v)$ is the subgraph induced by the vertices at distance at most $r$ from $v$, unlabelled except for the root $v$. Graphs $G,H$ have isomorphic $r$-neighbourhoods if there is a bijection $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ such that for every $v$ there is an isomorphism $N^{(G)}_r(v)\to N^{(H)}_r(\phi(v))$ mapping $v$ to $\phi(v)$; $G$ is reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods ($r$-reconstructible) if every graph with $r$-neighbourhoods isomorphic to those of $G$ is isomorphic to $G$ (the shotgun assembly problem). $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. At every radius $r$ there is a first phase transition around $p=n^{-\frac{2r+1}{2r}}$: below it every component lies inside an $r$-ball and $G$ is $r$-reconstructible, while slightly above it two disjoint paths on $2r+1$ vertices appear as components, which have the same $r$-neighbourhoods as disjoint $P_{2r}$ and $P_{2r+2}$, so $G$ is not $r$-reconstructible. The authors prove the second phase transition for all $r\ge3$: for $r=3$ it lies at $\frac{\log^2 n}{n(\log\log n)^3}$, and for $4\le r\le\log n$ at $\frac{\log n}{rn}$ (up to constant factors). For $r=2$ they show reconstructibility for $p\ge n^{-2/3-\delta}$ and non-reconstructibility for $\omega(n^{-5/4})\le p\le\frac13n^{-3/4}\log^{1/4}n$; for $r=1$, Huang and Tikhomirov showed reconstructibility for $n^{-1/2}\log^Cn\le p\le c$, and the authors show non-reconstructibility for $\omega(n^{-3/2})\le p\le\sqrt{\log n/(25n)}$. So the conjecture remains open for $r=1,2$.
notes: Proved within the paper for $r\geq 3$; remains open for $r=1,2$. The conjecture as universally quantified over all $r$ is therefore still open.

title: Question
statement_text: Determine when $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is 2-reconstructible. Is there a threshold around $n^{-3/4}$ (up to a polylogarithmic factor)?
context_text: For a graph $G$, a vertex $v$ and an integer $r\ge1$, the $r$-neighbourhood $N^{(G)}_r(v)$ is the subgraph induced by the vertices at distance at most $r$ from $v$, unlabelled except for the root $v$. Graphs $G,H$ have isomorphic $r$-neighbourhoods if there is a bijection $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ such that for every $v$ there is an isomorphism $N^{(G)}_r(v)\to N^{(H)}_r(\phi(v))$ mapping $v$ to $\phi(v)$; $G$ is reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods ($r$-reconstructible) if every graph with $r$-neighbourhoods isomorphic to those of $G$ is isomorphic to $G$ (the shotgun assembly problem). $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is the binomial random graph and 'with high probability' means with probability tending to 1 as $n\to\infty$. Since $\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ has diameter at most 2 for $p=\omega(\sqrt{\log n/n})$, it is then trivially 2-reconstructible. Gaudio and Mossel showed 2-reconstructibility w.h.p. for $n^{-3/5+\varepsilon}\le p\le n^{-1/2-\varepsilon}$ or $p\ge n^{-1/2+\varepsilon}$, and non-reconstructibility for $n^{-1+\varepsilon}\le p\le n^{-3/4-\varepsilon}$. The authors prove that $G\in\mathcal{G}(n,p)$ is w.h.p. 2-reconstructible if $p=o(n^{-5/4})$ or $p\ge n^{-2/3-\delta}$ for some constant $\delta>0$, and w.h.p. not 2-reconstructible if $p=\omega(n^{-5/4})$ and $p\le\frac13n^{-3/4}\log^{1/4}n$. The remaining gap is $n^{-3/4}\log^{1/4}n\lesssim p\lesssim n^{-2/3-\delta}$, while for every $r\ge3$ the authors determine the threshold of the second transition.
